analysis.one_liner: Lets courts break up large completed corporate mergers unless companies prove competition was preserved.
analysis.headline: Introduced April 29, 2026 by Sen. Booker with four Democratic cosponsors and referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee, where it has received no further action.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would rewrite merger law in two big ways. First, every merger worth $10 billion or more completed between January 2025 and January 2029 — the current presidential term — would have to be unwound, with the companies forced to sell off or separate what they bought, unless they could win a court ruling proving the deal did not hurt competition. Second, it would let federal agencies or state attorneys general unwind smaller deals if the approval process was tainted — for example by political pressure, behind-the-scenes lobbying, a revolving-door law firm, or a career staff recommendation that was ignored. It would also extend the deadline for antitrust lawsuits from four years to ten, and put fines, triple damages, and a court-appointed trustee behind the divestiture requirement.
analysis.who_benefits: Consumers and workers in markets dominated by a few large companies. If merged firms that raised prices or cut output are broken back apart, competition could push prices down and wages up. State attorneys general also gain a new tool to challenge tainted merger approvals.

how_it_helps.text: Acquirers in $10 billion-plus deals completed during the 2025–2029 covered period must divest the transaction unless they win a court exemption showing the deal stayed under concentration thresholds, prices and output matched what was promised, and no significant employment reduction occurred.

Agencies or state attorneys general can review smaller 'enforcement-lapse' deals and order divestiture if the approval was tainted by crimes, ignored staff recommendations, improper lobbying or ex parte contacts, presidential or cabinet statements favoring a buyer, conflicts of interest, revolving-door law firms, or foreign-government influence.

The bill extends the statute of limitations for private antitrust suits from four to ten years, requiring document preservation with adverse-inference and criminal sanctions, and provides daily fines up to $100,000 or 5% of deal value, triple damages, and a court-appointed divestiture trustee for noncompliance.

analysis.who_pays: Companies that completed or plan large mergers during the covered period would face forced unwinding of deals already approved and consummated, plus heavy litigation, compliance, and divestiture costs. Their shareholders bear the market value at risk. Merger advisers — law firms and lobbying firms — face new restrictions and liabilities.

drawbacks.text: The automatic divestiture rule covers every $10 billion-plus deal regardless of whether it actually harmed competition, so even companies that passed standard antitrust review must litigate under a shifted burden of proof and rigid numerical tests to keep their assets.

Retroactively unwinding consummated, lawful transactions creates enormous legal and financial uncertainty for any large company considering a merger, which supporters of existing merger practice would argue deters beneficial deals and investment.
The bill's own severability clause acknowledges that parts may be held unconstitutional, and courts applying it would face contested questions about retroactive penalties and due process.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: Where a big merger genuinely raised prices or cut output, forcing the companies back apart is a real, direct win for consumers, and the ten-year lawsuit window gives ordinary people and competitors a much longer chance to sue. But the design is blunt: a bright-line rule that unwinds every deal above $10 billion unless the company proves its innocence sweeps in many deals that did no competitive harm, and the retroactive reach over four years of transactions will draw constitutional challenges that could tie the whole thing up in court for years.

outcome.mechanism: Booker introduced the bill and it was referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee, which has taken no action since — no hearing, no markup, no vote.

narrative.text: Sen. Booker introduced S. 4434 on April 29, 2026, joined by Sens. Warren, Heinrich, Murphy, and Hirono, all Democrats.
The Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on the Judiciary the same day; no further action appears in the record.
The bill carries no Republican cosponsors, and the Senate Judiciary Committee has held no hearing or vote on it.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: As of now, no one has gained or lost — the bill is parked in committee and nothing has happened to it yet.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: No one yet — bill is parked

for.name: Sen. Cory Booker
for.role: U.S. Senator from New Jersey; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the CLEAN Mergers Act on April 29, 2026.

for.name: Sens. Elizabeth Warren, Martin Heinrich, Chris Murphy, and Mazie Hirono
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill at introduction; no Republican joined.

against.name: Senate Judiciary Committee
against.what_they_did: Has taken no action on the bill since referral on April 29, 2026 — no hearing, markup, or vote.

sides.party_line_note: All five sponsors are Democrats; the bill entered a Senate controlled by Republicans with no Republican cosponsor, and has drawn no recorded support across the aisle.

industries.industry: Large corporate acquirers in $10 billion-plus mergers
industries.note: The bill would force these companies to unwind deals worth $10 billion or more completed since January 2025 unless they prove in court the deals were harmless, with daily fines up to $100,000 or 5% of deal value and triple damages for knowing noncompliance. Shareholders of these firms bear the value at risk.

industries.industry: Corporate law firms and lobbying firms
industries.note: The bill disqualifies companies from keeping their deals if their lawyers provided pro bono legal services to settlement officials or if the firm employed a reviewing-agency political appointee in the prior year, and imposes document-preservation duties with sanctions and criminal referrals. It also lets courts refer failures to preserve evidence for prosecution.

industries.industry: Consolidated industries (hospitals, tech, telecom, transport, agriculture)
industries.note: Firms in any sector that grew by large acquisitions during the covered period face divestiture review, with the bill presuming structural remedies like breakup over other outcomes. Consumers in these concentrated markets would be the intended beneficiaries if prices fell after unwinding.

analysis.trajectory: With a Republican-controlled Senate, no Republican cosponsors, and no committee movement since the April 2026 referral, the bill is very unlikely to receive a hearing, markup, or floor vote before the 119th Congress ends in January 2027; this is the typical fate of partisan antitrust bills that stop at committee referral.
